Professional Medical Coding

The Language Payers Actually Understand

Medical coding is the translation layer between what a provider does clinically and what a payer will pay for. A note that says "removed inflamed appendix laparoscopically" only becomes billable once it is turned into the exact ICD-10-CM diagnosis code and CPT procedure code a payer's system recognizes. Get that translation wrong, even by one digit or a missing modifier, and a service the provider actually performed goes unpaid.

Since the Affordable Care Act tightened requirements around what providers must disclose to patients about the cost of care, accurate coding stopped being optional. Codes now have to hold up under payer scrutiny, patient billing transparency rules and compliance audits, all at once.

PMEX pairs coding software that flags likely codes from the documentation with credentialed human coders who review, correct and finalize every chart, so what reaches the payer reflects exactly what was done and is coded to survive an audit.

Coding Audits & Consultancy

Checking the Coding, Not Just Doing It

Even a strong coding team benefits from a second, independent pass. These three services keep coding accurate over time, not just accurate on day one.

Coders validate a sample of previously coded records, checking accuracy against documentation and current guidelines. Errors are corrected, patterns are flagged and reported, and the results feed directly back into coder training.

Documentation is the foundation every code rests on. This review checks whether the medical record actually supports the codes billed, catching vague notes, missing signatures, or gaps in medical necessity before a payer catches them instead.

Consultants review coding patterns across your patient population to apply the right codes consistently, supporting fair reimbursement and giving practice leadership a clearer view of population health and case complexity.

Questions

Medical Coding: Frequently Asked Questions

Coding turns clinical documentation into standardized diagnosis and procedure codes. Billing takes those codes and turns them into a submitted claim. Coding happens first, and billing depends entirely on getting it right.

Upcoding bills for a more complex or expensive service than was actually provided, which is a compliance risk. Undercoding bills for less than what was done, which quietly costs the practice revenue. Both are prevented by accurate, well-documented coding.

Yes. Coders are matched to your specialty, whether that means ICD-10-CM coding for oncology, CPT coding for orthopedics, or HCPCS Level II coding for durable medical equipment.

Hierarchical condition category coding links diagnosis codes to a patient's risk score. Accurate HCC coding ensures the risk adjustment factor reflects how complex a patient's care actually is, which directly affects Medicare Advantage reimbursement.

Both. Coding software scans documentation and suggests likely codes, then a certified coder reviews, corrects and finalizes every chart. Software speeds up the first pass, but a human always makes the final call.

Yes. PMEX can scale coding capacity up temporarily to clear a backlog, reducing DNFB and DNFC without requiring you to hire and train additional in-house coders.

CMI reflects the average complexity of the DRGs assigned to your patients. Accurate, complete coding ensures the true complexity of each case is captured, which supports fair reimbursement under Medicare and other DRG-based payers.
